5:23: Jesus is using the form of a question in order to teach. He wants to make the scribes and Pharisees reflect on the situation and realize something. There are many implications. For example, these religious leaders may take the question in the sense, “Which is easier to get away with saying?” The answer would be, “Your sins are forgiven,” because people do not expect visual proof of that, whereas if someone says, “Get up and walk,” and nothing happens, that proves the speaker does not have the power to heal. Jesus likely intends the question in a different sense: “Which is the easier way to deal with a situation like this?” It appears that the man’s sickness has something to do with his sins, because Jesus forgives them. In such a situation, it would not be sufficient to say, “Get up and walk,” since that would address the effect but not the cause. 23:29: Jesus is giving the reason why the women of Jerusalem should weep for themselves and their children, as he told them to do in the previous verse.
Jesus is using the term behold to get the women to focus their attention on what he is about to say.
Jesus is using the term days to refer to a specific time.
After speaking of women who were barren, that is, who did not have children, Jesus describes the same women in more detail. He is likely using repetition for emphasis.
These are two figures of speech in which Jesus is using one part of a person to represent the entire person.

The people do not want the mountains and hills to fall on them to harm them, but rather to protect them.
23:31: This is a figure of speech based on the idea that dry wood catches fire much more easily than moist wood. The fire, in turn, represents terrible things that people will experience. Jesus is saying that under the present relatively stable conditions, it was difficult for his enemies to arrest him and sentence him to death. In the future, conditions will become so desperate and chaotic that people will be able to do much worse things much more easily. He is probably referring to what conditions will be like during the siege and destruction of Jerusalem, which he described in 21:20–24.
Jesus does not expect the women to tell him what people will do in the future. Rather, he is using the question form for emphasis.
Jesus is using the term tree to refer to wood that comes from a tree.

Here rulers refers specifically to the Jewish leaders, not to the Roman rulers of the area.
Here the Jewish leaders are using irony. They do not really believe that Jesus saved other people.
In context, the Jewish leaders are implicitly referring to how Jesus saved others by doing miracles on their behalf.
The Jewish leaders are mockingly suggesting a hypothetical situation.
The implication is that Jesus ought to be able to save himself from dying on the cross, if he is the Messiah and can do miracles.

23:37: The soldiers are mockingly suggesting a hypothetical situation.

Together the two words answering and said mean that the second criminal rebuked the first one in response to what he said to Jesus.

The second criminal is using the word judgment to mean the punishment to which the first criminal was sentenced when the Romans pronounced judgment on him.
